deep_why: The core problem is ranking documents when users write long, multi-sentence queries with complex reasoning demands. The mathematical principle is that when you apply term-matching weights TO the query itself (not just documents), you automatically upweight rare, meaningful words that carry question intent. This works because rare words appear less frequently across all documents, so emphasizing them in the query makes the search more selective and precise. For long reasoning queries, this pruning effect is essential: without it, common filler words dominate the scoring, making every document seem equally relevant. By letting the weighting scheme treat the query as data to be analyzed, you solve the fundamental problem that long queries need intelligent word filtering to extract their true information need.

The core problem is evaluating whether conversational agents answer complex, multi-turn questions correctly when users evolve their preferences over several sessions. The mathematical principle is that a test collection with paired human conversations and automatic annotations creates a reproducible ground truth: different systems can be run through the same sequence of questions and judged against the same labels. This works because personalization requires measuring whether the agent's responses actually match what a specific user wanted at a specific turn, not just generic relevance. Building this dataset with multiple conversations per user and dynamic user models captures the fundamental challenge: a good agent must remember context, adapt its tone and depth to changing interests, and know when to ask clarifying questions. Without such a multi-session collection, evaluators cannot measure these nuances.

The core problem is bridging the gap between scientific abstracts that experts write for other experts and plain-language explanations that the public can understand and trust. The mathematical principle is that document-level alignment (pairing full abstracts to full summaries) preserves discourse structure—the logical flow, emphasis, and reasoning organization—which sentence-level pairs destroy. This works because simplifying text is not just word substitution; it requires reorganizing how ideas connect. A summary might reorder paragraphs, expand implicit assumptions, or remove jargon-heavy sections entirely. By providing pairs at the document scale, researchers can learn when and how to restructure information, not just which synonyms to substitute. This approach solves the real-world problem that public understanding requires not just simpler vocabulary but clearer logical scaffolding.

The core problem is ranking legal cases by relevance when citation links are absent and civil law systems rely on implicit factual and reasoning connections. The mathematical principle is that expert human judgment of relevance creates a proxy for the true legal reasoning chain: when trained legal professionals agree that two cases are related, their agreement reveals what properties matter (factual overlap, similar legal principles, shared argumentation). This works because civil-law systems (unlike common-law) do not maintain explicit citation networks, forcing ranking systems to learn relevance from raw text alone. Building annotations where experts jointly evaluate factual similarity AND legal reasoning structure grounds any ranking method in what lawyers actually recognize as meaningful. This solves the fundamental evaluation problem: without such anchoring, machine-learned relevance measures drift from what jurists know matters.

The core problem is understanding collaboration patterns and code reuse at the organizational level of GitHub, where individual projects are scattered across many groups. The mathematical principle is that a bipartite network (users on one side, repositories on the other, edges as contributions) precisely captures who does what: the structure itself reveals influence patterns, team formation, and dependency flow. This works because organizations operate as boundaries for governance and access control—studying them separately from raw user-repo pairs isolates the organizational effects (shared practices, internal standards, coordinated maintenance) that project-level analysis misses. By aggregating contributions at the organizational boundary and enriching edges with metadata (organization size, age, follower count), researchers can measure how organizational structure shapes collaboration itself. This network formulation solves the problem of understanding large-scale open-source as an ecosystem of interdependent groups, not just isolated projects.

The core problem is retrieving information in a low-resource dialect (Ehugbo) when existing multilingual models show a surprising failure: regional models familiar with the language family underperform global models trained on translation pairs. The mathematical principle is that training through explicit translation supervision forces the model to learn a shared, language-agnostic representation where equivalent meanings map to the same location in the scoring space. This works because cross-lingual alignment is not automatic from linguistic similarity; it requires seeing examples where the same meaning appears in different languages and learning to ignore language-specific noise. Regional models, trained on in-language text alone, never encounter this supervisory signal. By diagnosing this alignment gap through visualization and error analysis, the work reveals that dialect coverage alone is insufficient—you need the constraint that sentences with identical meaning must score near each other, regardless of language. This principle solves the fundamental problem that low-resource language search requires not local expertise but global alignment supervision.

The core problem is determining whether a language-model judge reliably scores retrieval-augmented generation systems when those systems cite their sources. The mathematical principle is that meta-evaluation—judging the judges against human assessments and against each other—creates a ground truth of judge quality. This works because judges can exhibit systematic flaws (favoring citations that sound confident regardless of accuracy, preferring longer responses, or bias toward their own format). By running the same responses through multiple judges and correlating their scores to human labels, you measure each judge's actual reliability, not just whether it produces reasonable-sounding explanations. This collection with pooled responses and known human judgments is the only way to audit judge behavior across their vulnerabilities. Solving this problem matters because judges are increasingly used to scale evaluation: you cannot trust a judge you have not validated against human consensus.

The core problem is evaluating query suggestion systems in a way that reflects how real users actually select suggestions: selectively and based on evolving intent, not by accepting the top suggestions blindly. The mathematical principle is that simulating user selection as an iterative choice task captures the feedback mechanism that occurs in actual search: a user examines each suggestion, judges whether it matches their emerging intent, and accepts or rejects it. This works because the quality of suggestions depends not just on ranking them well but on understanding which ranked items users would actually adopt. Simulating this selection process with a model trained to approximate human choice patterns converts static, offline evaluation (Does the true suggestion appear in the top-k?) into interactive evaluation (Would a user who sees this ranking actually select good suggestions?). This bridging of offline and online paradigms solves the practical problem that offline evaluation cannot measure real utility without modeling user decision-making.

The core problem is measuring language model performance on Traditional Mongolian when no systematic evaluation framework exists. The mathematical principle is that diverse test tasks (understanding and generation across reasoning, knowledge, and linguistic subtleties) collectively diagnose where a model fails: gaps in understanding reveal missing training signal, while semantic collapse in generation reveals inability to preserve meaning. This works because a single task (e.g., machine translation) conflates many sources of error; only by testing understanding separately from generation and sampling from multiple domains can you identify whether the failure is foundational (the model has not learned the language) or specific (it knows the language but cannot apply it in context). By using a hybrid construction method—combining verified translation adaptations, expert authoring, and semi-automated synthesis—the benchmark ensures coverage of the language's actual complexity, not just convenient test cases. This approach solves the problem that optimization blindly targets whatever benchmark exists; a well-designed benchmark for a low-resource language steers development toward genuine capability.

The core problem is detecting subtle narrative manipulation of cultural heritage on Wikipedia, where edits appear individually legitimate but accumulate to reframe agency and legitimacy over time. The mathematical principle is that paired revisions (before-and-after versions plus editorial context) allow fine-grained analysis of what changed and why: cumulative analysis of small shifts reveals patterns that individual edits conceal. This works because manipulation of cultural narrative rarely happens as a single, obvious vandalism; instead, it emerges through incremental reframing: removing an attribution here, adding qualifying language there, shifting agency through pronoun choice. No single change triggers alarms, but the cascade changes meaning. By providing the revision history with consistent annotations, researchers can detect this drift through statistical and linguistic analysis that single-version snapshots cannot. This dataset design solves the problem that Wikipedia's transparency paradox (all edits are public) actually obscures manipulation because users cannot easily compare many versions or visualize trends.

The core problem is organizing shared tasks where conversational search systems must interact with user simulators in real time, and both system and simulator must communicate in a standardized format. The mathematical principle is that a middleware API that exposes simulators as online endpoints and records interactions in a uniform schema eliminates the coordination burden: participants submit systems knowing they will receive requests in a standard format, and organizers collect responses knowing they have consistent structure. This works because shared tasks fail when technical friction overwhelms research contribution—if participants must build their own simulator integration, task overhead becomes prohibitive. By abstracting the simulator as a simple HTTP endpoint that accepts a query and returns suggestions, the system decouples simulator implementation from participant system design. This middleware converts the high-barrier online evaluation problem (systems and simulators must synchronize, interact, and log correctly) into a low-barrier one (call an API endpoint, receive data, return rankings). Solving this infrastructural problem enables the research community to standardize conversational search evaluation.

The core problem is ranking real-estate listings when relevance depends simultaneously on location, time (markets shift), and intrinsic quality, and raw listing data is too sensitive to release publicly. The mathematical principle is that aggregating listings into geo-temporal clusters (geographic regions at specific time periods) and computing stratified statistical summaries (percentiles of price over time) preserves market structure while eliminating individual privacy risk. This works because a user searching for apartments cares about neighborhoods and neighborhoods are inherently aggregates—the typical price in a district, how it changes seasonally, what transportation connects it. By providing cluster-level features and a transport-isolated price signal (the value attributable to location alone, separated from building quality), the dataset reveals what portion of price comes from where you are versus what you own. This decomposition solves the practical problem that explainable ranking requires understanding which features drive ranking, which requires disentangling confounded factors. The geo-temporal structure captures the real complexity: market value is not static but evolves as neighborhoods change.

The core problem is training and evaluating fraud-detection algorithms when real bank-transaction data are legally restricted and public alternatives distort financial semantics. The mathematical principle is that parameterized, scenario-driven simulation generates data that follows a transaction graph structure matching real systems: fraud patterns emerge naturally because the simulator models realistic sequences (normal transactions follow one temporal and structural pattern, fraudulent ones another). This works because fraud detection requires learning what transactions and patterns are anomalous; if synthetic data lacks realistic structure (temporal correlation, dependency on account type, seasonal variation), any model trained on it will overfit to artifacts and fail on real data. By offering both tabular records and transaction graphs, plus controllable fraud scenarios, the platform lets researchers understand which patterns matter: they can disable a scenario and watch accuracy drop, isolating what makes a scenario detectable. This approach solves the transferability problem: synthetic data that preserves financial semantics can substitute for sensitive real data, enabling reproducible, shareable research.

The core problem is building tip-of-the-tongue search benchmarks for languages beyond English when simulating realistic queries requires choosing which language to generate them in and which documents to draw from. The mathematical principle is that testing simulated queries against real user queries (measuring rank correlation of systems evaluated on each) validates whether the simulation method is accurate. This works because query simulation inherently involves linguistic and cultural choices: a Chinese user searching for a forgotten concept will naturally think in Chinese, so generating Chinese queries from English documents may fail to capture what they would actually search. By systematically varying the language of the source documents and the language of generation, then checking correlation against real users, researchers identify which combinations produce faithful simulation. This empirical validation is essential because query simulation, unlike document translation, has no ground truth—only correlation to actual search behavior reveals which methods generalize. Solving this problem enables researchers in multiple languages to build realistic retrieval benchmarks without the cost of collecting human tip-of-the-tongue queries.

The core problem is that conversational search research requires implementing complex pipelines (query reformulation, ranking, response generation) but existing systems are either locked in monolithic products or so specialized they cannot be reused. The mathematical principle is that modular architecture with single-file components and clear input-output contracts enables reuse: when each component specifies what it consumes and produces, developers can swap implementations and combine them without deep coupling. This works because conversational search needs personalization, long-context reasoning, and dynamic ranking—no single approach fits all scenarios. By providing 45+ off-the-shelf components (each one small, self-contained, and documented), the platform lowers the barrier to building prototypes: researchers can assemble a system quickly, test whether their new query understanding method helps, then publish the component for others to reuse. Production-ready infrastructure (credential management, telemetry, deployment support) bridges the gap from prototype to user evaluation. This modular platform solves the infrastructure problem that blocks conversational-search research: too much time on engineering, too little on innovation.
